tracks.title: Your agent is a config file in someones framework
tracks.text: Lesson five point two — authoring an agent. This one sits under agents, lesson five — so if a worker hired for outcomes is new to you, start there. Here is the opening idea. Your agent, in most frameworks, is a config file in someone elses framework. A Python class you subclass. A YAML schema with a validator. A vendor format only that one product reads. [sighs] And the most failure-prone part — the system prompt — is usually a string literal three imports deep, invisible in any diff that matters. None of it is inspectable. None of it is portable. [curious] Here, it is none of that. An agent definition is a plain org file… the same grammar as everything else. And the runtime that turns it into a worker is small enough to read in one sitting. That is this lesson — the file, and the runtime, with nothing hidden.

tracks.title: The definition
tracks.text: The definition. An agent definition is one org file describing a runnable agent. It has three parts. First… the first headline tagged agent. Second… a properties drawer carrying four keys — I D, model, toolkits, and tagline. And third… a heading that reads, exactly, star star System prompt — whose body becomes the prompt. That is the whole contract. No schema, no decorator, no build step. The agent is discovered like a toolkit — by a tag — and run on the same substrate as everything else. Let me read you a complete one, top to bottom. Title line — analyst agent. Then a headline, Data Analyst, tagged agent. Its drawer sets I D to analyst… model to a small cheap model called mimo… a one-line tagline… and toolkits to three names — shell, w b, and sandbox. Then the heading, star star System prompt, and under it a short paragraph — you are analyst, a clean-room runtime agent, use the shell jq command to extract JSON, persist findings with w b memory remember, and call done when complete. [curious] Twenty-five lines… and nothing else. Point the runtime at that file, and it has a worker.

tracks.title: What the runtime actually reads
tracks.text: Now — what the runtime actually reads. The parser is one module, and it is seventy-three lines total. You can hold the whole thing in your head, so let us. Picture a short pipeline, left to right. On the left, the org file — plain text. It flows into o-q-l dot wasm, the kernel — the very same WebAssembly component that parses workbooks. The kernel hands back one record per headline, each carrying its level, title, tags, properties, and body. Next box — find the first node whose tags contain the word agent. That is the whole of discovery. The tag IS the registration. And the last box on the right — a five-field record — I D, model, toolkits, tagline, and the system prompt. That record is everything the runtime knows about your agent. Three mechanics fall out of that. First — discovery is a tag, the same move that finds toolkit nodes. Second — the four properties come straight off the drawer, and toolkits is whitespace-split, so shell w b sandbox becomes three names. Third — a missing toolkits list is not an error… it just defaults to empty. [excited] Because the kernel does the parsing, an agent def has no format of its own. It is org… read by the org reader.

tracks.title: The System prompt rule
tracks.text: The System prompt rule — and this is the one to get exactly right. The prompt is everything under a heading that reads star star System prompt, that exact title, up to the next level-one-or-two heading — a single star or a double star. Here is the part people miss. Deeper headings — three stars — do NOT end the prompt. They are part of it, by design. Picture a real def as a skeleton. A headline tagged agent — parsed for its properties only. Some prose right under it — that prose is NOT in the prompt. Then star star System prompt — the prompt starts after this line. Then three three-star children — Ground rules, Tooling, Orientation budget — and every one of them stays INSIDE the prompt. And finally a single-star heading, Working notes — that one ends the prompt, so it is out. So a serious def can nest a whole operations manual as three-star children and have all of it land in one system prompt. Now — the fallback. What if there is no System prompt heading at all? The parser does not run the agent empty. It falls back to the node body — everything after the first end-of-drawer line. And the comment naming why is a real production scar. It reads… an agent authored as a plain def should not silently run prompt-less. This bit bit-em-el — the crew ran with empty prompts and all imitated desk. [sighs] That actually happened. Agents shipped with no recognized heading, the runtime handed each an empty prompt, and with nothing to be… they all imitated one of their number, and one fabricated. So here is the failure table, and its verdict in one line. Star star System prompt, spelled exactly — you get the body, through the three-star children, to the next heading. Capital P on Prompt — no match, falls back to the node body. Any other title — no match, falls back. No heading at all — the node body, better than empty but not what you meant. The lesson is small and absolute… write star star System prompt, exactly.

tracks.title: Toolkits become a prompt index
tracks.text: Next — toolkits become a prompt index. This is the second surprise. Declaring toolkits — say, git and sandbox — does NOT paste two manuals into your prompt. At run time the runtime turns that list into a tiny index and appends it — taglines and skill names, nothing more. Picture the flow, left to right. Your declared list… is looked up against the toolkit root directory. Each toolkit found becomes one row — its tagline from the manifest, plus the first eight skill names, with a plus-N-more if there are extras. That whole block is appended as the literal last thing in the prompt. And off to the side, dashed — the skill bodies themselves are fetched only on demand, when the agent needs one, through the w b tool. Index in the prompt… manuals on demand. Let me read the real shape. A heading — hash hash Toolkits. Then a line that says — you have these toolkits, and before using one, read the relevant skill by calling the w b tool with toolkit show. Then the rows. Git — host-brokered commit and push for agent workdirs — skills, overview and publish-flow. And sandbox… not installed. Three things to take. First — that header text teaches the read-deeper move, naming the exact command, so the agent learns to go deeper without you spelling it out. Second — a misspelled or missing toolkit does not crash the run, it shows as not-installed, a breadcrumb instead of a stack trace. Third — an empty toolkits list appends nothing at all… so a toolkit-less agents prompt is exactly what you wrote, not a byte more.

tracks.title: From parse to a live loop
tracks.text: From parse… to a live loop. Parsing makes a record. The run function turns it into a running agent — it assembles the prompt, your text plus the toolkit index, and hands it to the loop with the task. Two details matter to an author. First — the model is a default you can override. The model in your def is passed as a default, not a mandate. The callers choice wins. And if nothing names a model, it falls through an environment variable to a built-in. So you write the model you intend… and an operator can swap it per run without touching your file. Second — the loop is bounded. The agent calls the model, runs the tools it asked for, appends the results, and loops — finishing when it stops calling tools or calls done, capped at twelve steps by default. Every tool call is bounded at a hundred and fifty seconds, and every step is logged. The loops internals are their own lesson. What you need here is the tool surface. So here is the verdict of the tool table, without reading every row. Every agent gets the shell — an in-WASM shell, jq and grep and sort, with pipes, but no operating-system process. Every agent gets search over its workdir, the w b CLI, fetch and web-search, a file-issue seam, and the workspace read-write plus done. And then — only trusted agents, the ones marked exec-true — additionally get git, publish, and image generation. [curious] And this reconciles the parent lessons line that an agent gets exactly one tool — a shell. The shell IS the primary tool, the place it thinks by doing. Everything else is the host-brokered membrane around it — ways to read and write, commit and publish, end the run. No path anywhere runs native operating-system code… the old real-bash hatch was deleted on purpose. A trusted def gets git and publish — that is a grant. Which is why you author an exec def like production code.

tracks.title: One def, four doors
tracks.text: One def… four doors. This one is a depth rung — skippable — but it answers a real puzzle. How can a def say trust the lifecycle line, when that line appears nowhere in the org file? Picture four doors into one room. The same run function is called from four places, and all four flow into one box — parse, inject, run — and then into the agent loop. Door one — the keeper tick — runs a def on an interval inside a tenants git working directory, and it prepends lines like MODE and LIFECYCLE wake-audit to the task before the agent ever sees it. THAT is why a def can trust those lines as a given, even though it never wrote them. Door two — a fleet worker — runs one member of a manifest, each member pointing at its own def file. Door three — H-T-T-P — runs a def per request, the long-horizon one letting you poll or stream while it works. And door four — the autopoet — runs through the exact same path, supervised and time-bounded. The point for an author — your def is data, and the caller supplies the context. The workdir… the task framing… the trust level. Four different jobs, one parse, one run path.

tracks.title: Reading a real def — Waldo
tracks.text: Reading a real def — Waldo. The analyst is twenty-five lines. The other end of the honest range is Waldo, the agent behind this projects landing site… at four hundred and fifty-two lines. And reading it teaches the real lesson of authoring — a production def is an operations manual, and the three-star nesting is exactly what keeps the whole manual inside one prompt. Every section is a three-star child under System prompt, so every one is in the prompt. Let me name them. First… identity and mandate. Second… a territory map, with explicit hands-off zones. Third… the canon it holds, referenced not re-pasted. Fourth… the staged design process for a single run. Fifth… a board protocol, a native org to-do board it works from. Sixth… the cadence, with a commit-tag taxonomy. Seventh… ground rules — never fabricate, the prompt-injection boundary, the no-work rule. Eighth… tooling. And ninth… an orientation budget, a hard cap on how much it reads before it acts. That tooling section is the one to dwell on, because it shows a def documenting its own sandbox without flinching. It says, in plain words… no l-s — it is not implemented — read the manifest. [chuckles] Waldo tells the model the truth about its environment, rather than letting it discover the gaps by failing. And one honest seam — Waldos prompt says it runs every fifteen minutes and dies at a twelve-minute wall clock. Neither number lives in the file. They are deployment config. The def DESCRIBES the cadence to the model… the environment ENFORCES it. A duplication the author keeps in sync by hand — and the cleanest example of the limits we cover next.

tracks.title: The honest limits
tracks.text: The honest limits. The format is intentionally thin, and thin formats have sharp edges. Here they are, plainly. First — the heading typo is silent. Capital P on Prompt, or any other title, does not match, and instead of erroring the runtime falls back to the node body. Better than empty… not what you wrote. This is the single most common way to ship a subtly-wrong agent. Second — the agents tagline is parsed but cosmetic. It is read into the record, but the runtime has no consumer for it beyond the parse. Third — a type property is ignored entirely. The real analyst file declares one, and the parser never reads it. Fourth — an undeclared toolkit does not fail, it just renders as not-installed in the index. Fifth — cadence and timeout live in the environment, not the def, so your prose can drift from reality. Waldos every-fifteen-minutes is a claim… the interval variable is the fact. Sixth — the parser cannot gate prompt quality. It reads structure. It cannot make your mandate good. And seventh — a def is trusted input. An exec def gets git and publish, real capabilities. [curious] Author it like production code… because in the only sense that matters, it is.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Do I need a System prompt heading? No — but you want one. Without it, the prompt is the node body, and only the explicit heading survives once you add other sections. Can two agent nodes share one file? Only the first is parsed — the parser finds one tagged node and stops. Fleet members live in separate files. How do I override the model without editing the def? The model in your file is a default — the callers choice wins, and an environment variable backs it up. What about a toolkit I did not declare? Declaration controls the INDEX in your prompt, not access — the w b tool can read any installed toolkit either way. And — how big should a def be? As big as the responsibility, no bigger. Twenty-five lines for the analyst… four hundred and fifty for Waldo. The size tracks what the agent is on the hook for, and most defs sit far closer to the analyst.

tracks.title: Keep going
tracks.text: So — that is authoring. An agent is one org file. A tagged headline… four properties… and a heading whose body is the prompt, three-star children and all. No schema, no class, no build step — just a file you can diff, send, and read aloud. [curious] You can write one now. The way on is short. The parent — agents, lesson five — for what a worker is. Loops — for the run your def feeds. Context repo — for where its memory lives. And toolkits — for what that little index points at. Everything you just learned… is one plain file, read by the same kernel that reads everything else.
